episode: Why The Titanic Can Never Be Raised
style_instruction: A deep-voiced documentary narrator. Gravelly authority with serious urgency. Neutral American accent, slightly weathered. Moderate pace — not rushed, but crisp. Brief, natural pauses between sentences. Let the weight come from tone and emphasis, not extended silence. Cold, intimate, pressing.

scenes.label: Hook
scenes.transcript: [serious, urgent] In 1912, the most famous ship in history sank to the bottom of the Atlantic. [short pause] Over a century later—it's still there. Exactly where it fell. [intense] Not because nobody wants to bring it up. Because it is physically... impossible.

scenes.label: The Depth
scenes.transcript: [serious, urgent] The Titanic rests at three thousand, eight hundred meters below the surface. [short pause] That's two point three seven miles—straight down—into the North Atlantic. [pause] To put that in perspective: stack nine Eiffel Towers on top of each other. [short pause] You still wouldn't reach it. It's deeper than most nuclear submarines can even operate. [slow, quiet] And down there? Zero sunlight. Eternal darkness.

scenes.label: Crushing Pressure
scenes.transcript: [serious, urgent] At that depth, the pressure is three hundred and eighty times greater than at sea level. [short pause] Five thousand, five hundred pounds—per square inch—pressing on everything. [pause] Imagine fifty elephants balanced on a single postage stamp. [short pause] That is the force the Titanic endures. Every second. [pause] Even military submarines get crushed long before reaching this depth. [slow] A styrofoam cup taken down there? [short pause] It shrinks to the size of a thimble.

scenes.label: Scale and Wreckage
scenes.transcript: [serious, urgent] The Titanic weighs fifty-two thousand tons. It's two hundred and sixty-nine meters long—longer than two and a half football fields end to end. [short pause] But here's the thing. [pause] It didn't sink in one piece. [intense] The ship split apart during the sinking. [short pause] The two sections landed six hundred meters apart on the ocean floor. [pause] Surrounding them—over one hundred thousand objects, scattered across twenty-seven square kilometers of seabed. [slow, quiet] There is no ship to raise. There is a graveyard of wreckage.

scenes.label: Fragility
scenes.transcript: [serious, urgent] After one hundred and thirteen years in saltwater under extreme pressure—the steel is brittle as a cracker. [short pause] A bacteria called Halomonas titanicae is actively eating the wreck right now. [pause] It produces rust formations that are slowly consuming the hull from the inside. [short pause] Scientists estimate the Titanic will be completely gone within twenty years. [pause] If anyone attempted to lift it today— [slow, intense] it would disintegrate before reaching the surface.

scenes.label: Failed Plans
scenes.transcript: [dry, serious] People have been trying to solve this for over a century. Here's how that went. [short pause] Fill it with ping-pong balls. [pause] The balls get crushed before they reach the wreck. [short pause] Attach balloons to the hull. [pause] Same problem—implode on the way down. [short pause] Freeze it in liquid nitrogen. [pause] Would require five hundred thousand tons of nitrogen. [short pause] Just build a crane and lift it. [pause] The project would cost over a hundred billion dollars. Minimum. [slow] And even if we somehow pulled it off— [short pause] where would you put a two-hundred-and-sixty-nine-meter deteriorating shipwreck?

scenes.label: The Real Reason — Outro
scenes.transcript: [serious, urgent] But beyond all the physics and the engineering—there is one more reason the Titanic stays where it is. [pause] Over fifteen hundred people never made it to the surface that night. [short pause] Many of them are still down there. [pause] The wreck is—legally and morally— [slow] a cemetery. [pause] Governments. Families. Historians. They all agree: [slow] some things should stay where they rest. [long pause] [whispers] The Titanic chose the ocean floor. [pause] [whispers] And the ocean floor chose to keep it.
